name: Design a Live Video Streaming Platform
intent: Take a broadcaster's live video, turn it into several qualities in real time, and deliver it to millions of viewers a few seconds behind the camera, even when a stream suddenly goes viral.
codeTitle: a rendition ladder, shielded segment delivery, latency and failover
finalIntro: One stream from a broadcaster's camera to a viewer's screen, including an ingest failure.
prompt: Design a platform where anyone can broadcast live video and others watch it. Broadcasters push a stream from their encoder, viewers watch on phones, browsers and TVs over networks of very different speeds, and a single stream can go from a few hundred to a few million viewers within minutes. Keep the delay between camera and screen low without making playback stutter.
functional: Accept a live stream from a broadcaster over RTMP or SRT, with a stream key
Produce several qualities of the stream (a bitrate ladder) in real time
Let each viewer watch at the quality their network can sustain, and switch while playing
Offer the stream over HLS and DASH so that every device can play it
Show the live viewer count and let the broadcaster see the stream's health
Keep a recording that can be watched later as video on demand
nonFunctional: Glass-to-glass latency of about 3 to 10 seconds, depending on the mode the broadcaster chooses
Playback that rarely stalls, even when the viewer's bandwidth changes
Survive the loss of an ingest server or a transcoder without the stream ending
Handle millions of concurrent viewers on one stream and hundreds of thousands of viewers' worth of new joins per minute
Keep the origin's load almost independent of the number of viewers
Use compute and bandwidth efficiently, since transcoding and egress are the main costs

firstAttempt.text: One media server per broadcaster. The encoder pushes RTMP to it, and the same server transcodes the video if needed, cuts it into HLS files and serves those files to every viewer directly over HTTP.
limits: The server's network card is the limit: 2,000 viewers at 3 Mbps is already 6 Gbps
Transcoding and serving compete for the same CPU, so a surge of viewers makes the video itself stutter
Every viewer far from the server pays a long round trip for each segment
If the server or the broadcaster's connection drops, the stream ends for everybody
Only one quality exists, so viewers on slow networks stall and viewers on fast ones see poor video

steps.title: Accept the stream on an ingest tier with a standby
steps.problem: A single server that takes the broadcaster's connection is a single point of failure, and the connection from the broadcaster's home network is itself unreliable.
steps.fix: Broadcasters connect to an ingest gateway near them, found by DNS or anycast, using RTMP or SRT with a stream key that is checked before any media is accepted. SRT adds retransmission and encryption on a lossy network, where RTMP over TCP stalls on packet loss. A second gateway in another zone is ready to take the same stream key, and the encoder reconnects to it automatically if the first connection drops. The gateway only receives, checks and forwards the stream, so it needs little CPU.
steps.tradeoff: A dropped connection becomes a short pause instead of the end of the stream. The standby costs idle capacity, a reconnect still loses a few seconds of media, and the encoder must be configured to retry, which not every consumer encoder does well.

steps.title: Transcode a bitrate ladder in real time
steps.problem: A single quality cannot suit a 4G phone and a living-room TV, and transcoding on the server that receives the stream makes ingest fail whenever the CPU is busy.
steps.fix: The gateway writes the incoming stream into a short, ordered buffer, and a pool of transcoders reads it and produces a ladder, for example 1080p at 6 Mbps, 720p at 3 Mbps, 480p at 1.2 Mbps and 240p at 0.4 Mbps. Every rendition is cut at the same keyframe times (a group of pictures of two seconds), which is what lets a player switch quality at a segment boundary without a glitch. If a transcoder dies, another picks up the buffer from the last position. Video from small streams can skip the ladder when nobody is watching.
steps.tradeoff: Each viewer gets video that fits their network, and the transcoders can fail and restart independently of ingest. Real-time transcoding is the largest compute cost of the platform, it adds a few hundred milliseconds of delay, and a ladder must be tuned so that it is not wasteful for content that compresses well.

steps.title: Cut into short segments and keep them on an origin
steps.problem: Viewers need plain files that any HTTP cache can store, not a long-lived media connection to a server that does the work for each of them.
steps.fix: A packager cuts each rendition into segments of two seconds, wraps them in fMP4 or MPEG-TS, and writes them to an origin store together with a playlist (HLS) or manifest (DASH) that lists the newest segments. A viewer's player downloads the playlist, then the segments in order, and measures its download speed to pick the rendition for the next one. The same segments are kept for recording and video on demand, and the playlist is a small file that changes every two seconds.
steps.tradeoff: Delivery becomes ordinary cacheable HTTP, which scales like any website and works on every device. Latency is now at least a few segment durations, since a segment exists only when it is complete, and shorter segments cost more requests and a less efficient encoding.

steps.title: Fan out through a CDN with an origin shield
steps.problem: A million viewers asking the origin for each two-second segment would take it down, and every viewer far from it would pay a long round trip.
steps.fix: Viewers fetch from CDN edges close to them. An edge that misses does not go to the origin: it asks a regional origin shield, which is a cache in front of the origin that all edges share. Both tiers coalesce requests, so when thousands of viewers ask for the same new segment at once, a single request goes upstream and the rest wait for it. The origin then sees roughly one request per rendition and segment, whatever the audience. Segments are immutable and cached for their lifetime, and the playlist gets a lifetime of about one segment.
steps.tradeoff: The origin's load no longer depends on the number of viewers, and most requests are answered nearby. The shield adds a hop on the first miss, a misconfigured cache key can make every edge miss at once, and the CDN is a large bill and a dependency, so big platforms use more than one.

steps.title: Trade latency against buffering with parts and hold-back
steps.problem: With two-second segments and a player that holds three of them, the viewer sees the action about nine seconds late, which is too slow for a live auction or a chat that reacts to the video.
steps.fix: The packager publishes each segment in parts of about half a second as they are encoded (low-latency HLS, or chunked CMAF in DASH). A playlist server holds a playlist request open until the next part exists, so the player learns about new media immediately instead of polling, and the CDN passes the parts on while the segment is still being written. The player keeps a hold-back of about three parts rather than three segments, which gives roughly three seconds end to end. Broadcasters choose the mode: a normal latency stream stays at two-second segments and a deeper buffer, which is cheaper and more robust.
steps.tradeoff: Latency falls from about nine seconds to about three, and a chat can react to the video. The request rate per viewer rises about fourfold, a small buffer means any network wobble causes a stall, and not all players and CDNs support parts well.

steps.title: Survive spikes and count viewers
steps.problem: A famous streamer going live gives the CDN a sudden crowd of new viewers who all miss the cache together, and the broadcaster still wants a live viewer count without a database write for every viewer.
steps.fix: Viewers send a heartbeat every thirty seconds to a counter that keeps approximate per-stream counts in sharded in-memory sets and sums them, so the shown number is a second or two stale and slightly approximate. A spike control watches the counts and the cache hit ratio, pre-warms the shield with the first segments of a stream that is about to be announced, and when capacity is short it sheds the top rendition first or lengthens the playlist lifetime so that viewers drop to lower quality instead of failing. Transcoders and packagers scale on the number of live streams, while CDN capacity is reserved ahead of big events.
steps.tradeoff: A surge degrades quality gracefully instead of breaking playback, and the counter is cheap. The displayed number is not exact, shedding visibly lowers quality for everybody during the worst moments, and pre-warming and reserved capacity cost money even when the event is a flop.

failures.scenario: The ingest server fails in the middle of a stream
failures.impact: The broadcaster's connection drops, and without a plan the stream has a gap of unknown length or ends altogether.
failures.answer: The encoder reconnects to the standby with the same stream key. Timestamps continue from the media clock, so the packager resumes on the next segment boundary and players see a discontinuity marker instead of a restart. A viewer who holds three segments of buffer rides through a gap of a few seconds without stalling. For the most important streams, the encoder sends to two gateways at once, both feed the pipeline with identical segmentation, and no gap appears.

failures.scenario: A transcoder crashes while serving a popular stream
failures.impact: The higher renditions stop being produced, and viewers on them stall within a few seconds.
failures.answer: Transcoders are stateless readers of the raw stream buffer, so a replacement resumes from the last finished segment, and a lease stops two transcoders from writing the same rendition. While it catches up the player's adaptive logic falls back to a rendition that is still being produced. Only one of two concurrent transcoders may publish, using a fencing token on the segment number.

failures.scenario: A stream goes viral and a million viewers join in a minute
failures.impact: New viewers all request the playlist and the newest segment from edges that have not got them yet, and the herd lands on the origin.
failures.answer: Request coalescing at the edge and the shield turns the herd into one request per rendition and segment. The playlist is cached for about one segment duration. If the shield is still struggling, the spike control removes the top rendition from the playlist, so that new viewers start at a lower quality, and sheds requests with a short retry-after instead of letting the queue grow.

failures.impact: The segment they are downloading arrives slower than it plays, and the buffer drains toward a stall.
failures.answer: The player measures the throughput of each segment and switches down a rung of the ladder at the next boundary, which works because every rendition is cut at the same instants. It keeps a safety margin in the throughput estimate and prefers to switch down quickly and up slowly. A player with a short low-latency hold-back has less room to react, so it may fall back to normal latency instead of stalling.

alternatives.title: How the video reaches the viewer

options.name: HLS or DASH over HTTP and a CDN
options.pro: Scales like a website, works on every device, and adapts quality per viewer
options.con: Several seconds of latency, even with low-latency parts

options.name: WebRTC to every viewer
options.pro: Under a second of latency and two-way interaction
options.con: Stateful connections to media servers, expensive to scale to millions, and no plain HTTP cache

options.name: Chunked HTTP with a custom player
options.con: A custom player to maintain on every platform

alternatives.pick: HLS and DASH with low-latency parts by default, and WebRTC only for small, interactive rooms.

alternatives.title: How to get the stream in

options.name: RTMP
options.pro: Supported by almost every encoder and streaming app
options.con: TCP only, old, and not encrypted unless wrapped

options.name: SRT
options.pro: Handles packet loss and jitter with retransmission, and is encrypted

options.name: WebRTC (WHIP)
options.pro: Sends from a browser with sub-second latency
options.con: Lower quality control and harder to scale ingest

alternatives.pick: RTMP for reach, SRT for professional broadcasts over bad links, and WHIP for browser studios.

alternatives.title: When to transcode

options.name: Always, the full ladder
options.pro: Every viewer gets a good rendition from the first second
options.con: Wastes compute on streams that have no viewers

options.name: On demand, when viewers appear
options.pro: Costs compute only for streams that are watched
options.con: The first viewers wait or get the source quality

options.name: Source quality only for small streams
options.con: Viewers on slow networks cannot watch

alternatives.pick: A full ladder for partners and any stream with an audience, a reduced ladder for small streams, and more renditions as the audience grows.

alternatives.title: Segment length

options.name: 6 seconds
options.pro: Few requests, efficient encoding, very robust playback
options.con: About 25 seconds behind the camera with a three-segment hold-back

options.name: 2 seconds
options.pro: Around 9 seconds of latency with a moderate request rate
options.con: Three times the requests of six-second segments

options.name: Half-second parts inside 2-second segments
options.con: Four times the requests again, and less room to absorb network trouble

alternatives.pick: Two-second segments as the default, parts for streams that need interaction, and long segments for streams that value reliability over latency.
